newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen lacking room to tighten money policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen lacking room to tighten money policy.

text.p: Taiwan's flat money supply growth in January has left the central bank little room to tighten monetary policy despite concerns that the booming stock market was attracting too much money, economists said on Monday.
Taiwan's M2 money supply grew 9.35 percent in January compared to January 1996 under a newly adjusted definition of the island's broadest money supply measure, the central bank said on Monday.

The year-on-year increase put M2 growth within the central bank's 9-14 percent target zone for the first time since August 1995 and slightly above the average 9.1 percent rise forecast by a February 21 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.

Economists said the new M2 definition, which expands the category to include several additional types of money, would add one to 1.5 percentage points to M2 growth -- all but ensuring that January's M2 growth would fall into the target zone.
"Despite falling within the central bank's target zone, January's M2 growth was still too slow to help a recovering economy," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
The island's gross domestic product grew a year-on-year 6.62 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, up from 5.12, 5.42 and 5.61 percent, respectively, in the first, second and third quarters.

Central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Saturday, after the local stock index had climbed to a six-year high, that investors should exercise caution in a market that has risen more than 1,000 points in 1997.
Hsu's comments led to a 1.29-percent fall in the market on Monday, triggering concerns the bank would tighten its monetary policy.
But economists said they saw little or no room for the central bank to tighten policy.

They said January's money supply growth was slow considering that money demand in January and February -- ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year holiday (which fell on February 7 in 1997) -- is usually higher than demand during other periods.

"January's flat 9.35 percent M2 growth showed the economic recovery is still very slow," said HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang. "And there is no room for the central bank to tighten its monetary policy."
Economists said the central bank had issued the warning in an attempt to direct the island's loose liquidity to other economic activities and to prevent the stock market from hoarding too much money.

"The central bank is unlikely to reverse its current stable-to-loose monetary policy, but simply is trying to lead the loose liquidity to boost investment, the property market or other economic activities," said Nomura's Huang.
Economists noted that January's M1 money supply growth rose 11.26 percent year-on-year, higher than December's 8.21 percent growth, indicating rising money flows to the stock market.
According to the central bank's definition, M1A was cash, checking accounts and passbook deposits and M1B was M1A plus savings accounts.
"If M1B growth continued to expand because of the bullish stock market, the central bank might conduct open market operations to slightly control liquidity," Huang said.
"But it will not raise banks' reserve requirements," she added.
The central bank on Monday issued T$5 billion (US$182 million) in negotiable certificates of deposits to mop up excess liquidity.
